summary:
PLANET FITNESS ASTRObreath AI is an autonomous health monitoring system created for deep-space astronauts who lack real-time medical support and monitoring from Earth. It is created using NASA and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) research combining, continuous wearable and cabin data (heart rate, oxygen, radiation, CO2) with quick and non-invasive checks that also include breath analysis, blood pressure, and also eye pressure tests.

By using an interactive Astronaut Body Map, our platform learns each crew member’s personal VOC baseline to detect subtle health shifts early. When an anomaly or an environmental risk occurs, the system verifies the data then determines the severity of the situation and guides the astronaut through a simple 3-step Action Protocol: how to re-measure, why it matters and what immediate steps to take. It also includes interactive breathing exercises, lighting adjustment, music session and so on to reduce isolation stress and stabilise heart rate.

While it’s primary functions are built for Artemis and Mars missions, ASTRObreath AI can also serve Earth, giving remote communities and chronic respiratory patients an accessible and non-invasive self-care tool.
details:
Project Overview: PLANET FITNESS ASTRObreath AI Application

PLANET FITNESS ASTRObreath AI is an offline-first, autonomous astronaut health monitoring and clinical decision support system (DSS) built for long-duration deep-space missions, such as Artemis lunar habitats and Mars transit, where communication delays prevent real-time Earth support and crew members are not medical doctors. Grounded in NASA Human Research Program (HRP) hazards, NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) datasets, and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) radiation research, the platform unifies cabin environmental telemetry, non-invasive breath biomarker screening, edge PyTorch LSTM time-series analysis, and step-by-step clinical guidance into a single medical-aerospace interface.

What It Does & How It Works

·       Personalized Baseline Calibration (Sync with OSDR / NLSP): Before and during a mission, the system ingests historical spaceflight datasets from NASA OSDR, the Ames Life Sciences Data Archive (ALSDA), GeneLab, the NASA Life Sciences Portal (NLSP), and RadLab via JSON/CSV payloads. Using these records alongside time-series anomaly modeling, ASTRObreath AI calibrates individualized physiological safety thresholds rather than relying on broad Earth-based averages.

·       Dual-Mode Telemetry (LIVE SENSOR vs. SPOT-CHECK): The platform distinguishes between passive continuous environmental/flow monitoring and active periodic breath exams:

o   Continuous Live Sensors: Tracks real-time respiratory airflow and tidal volume (via the Sensirion SFM3000), cumulative space radiation dose (Galactic Cosmic Rays and Solar Particle Events), and Cabin Atmosphere telemetry, including CO2 partial pressure (<= 3 mmHg), CO2 concentration (<= 2000 ppm), temperature, and relative humidity (via the Bosch BME280).

o   Guided Manual Spot-Checks: Prompts astronauts through 10-second non-invasive exhaled breath Volatile Organic Compound (VOC) spot-checks sampled at 200 ms intervals across six targeted biomarkers: Acetone (<1.5 ppm), Isoprene (40 to 150 ppb), Hexanal (<2.0 ppb), Nonanal (<1.0 ppb), Ethane (<3.0 ppb), and Pentane (<5.0 ppb).

o   Interactive Astronaut Body Map & Cascading Diagnostics: A static, high-contrast anatomical wireframe displays color-coded health status ('Nominal', 'Caution', 'Critical') across the Lungs & Respiratory (Hexanal, Nonanal, respiratory rate, tidal volume), Metabolic & Oxidative Stress (Acetone, Ethane, Pentane), and Musculoskeletal (Isoprene) systems. When environmental telemetry drifts (such as rising cabin CO2 or elevated radiation flux) or a breath curve spikes, the software cross-checks metrics, triages severity, and directs the astronaut to perform a targeted breath spot-check to confirm the physiological impact.

o   Plain-English 3-Step Clinical Action Protocol: Whenever a VOC or environmental reading crosses a critical threshold, a modal automatically guides the non-physician astronaut through three clear sections:
1. How to Take Measurement: Simple instructions for running a 10-second exhalation spot-check on the handheld ASTRObreath sensor unit.
2. Why It Matters: Concise explanation linking the abnormal biomarker to spaceflight hazards, including hepatic ketogenesis and caloric exhaustion (Acetone), skeletal muscle exertion or microgravity atrophy (Isoprene), airway epithelial irritation from spacesuit off-gassing or lunar regolith dust (Hexanal and Nonanal), or radiation-induced cellular lipid peroxidation (Ethane and Pentane).
3. What to Do: Numbered, VOC-triggered countermeasures, including consuming 300 kcal of complex carbohydrates to halt ketosis, inspecting spacesuit seals and cycling cabin HEPA/activated carbon scrubbers, retreating to a radiation storm shelter and administering antioxidants, or adjusting EVA workload intensity, with one-tap logging to an offline mission sync queue.

Benefits of the Project

·       Zero-Latency Medical Autonomy: Operates 100% locally offline on spacecraft edge hardware (ESP32) and habitat computers, eliminating life-threatening delays during communication blackouts or 14-to-22-minute Mars signal latencies.

·       Non-Invasive Early Anomaly Detection: Replaces bulky, invasive blood draws with a 10-second breath test to detect metabolic exhaustion, airway inflammation, muscle breakdown, and radiation-induced oxidative stress early.

·       Reduced Cognitive Overload in Emergencies: Replaces raw, fragmented sensor logs with scannable color codes, clickable organ hotspots, and plain-English 3-step action protocols so astronauts can respond calmly under stress.

·       Unified Human & Environmental Telemetry: Connects exhaled breath biomarkers directly with cabin CO2 and space radiation monitoring in one cohesive clinical workflow.

Intended Impact

·       Protecting Deep-Space Crews: Directly addresses NASA HRP risks across all five hazards of human spaceflight (space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile closed environments), enabling Earth-independent medical self-reliance on Artemis lunar missions and future Mars expeditions.

·       Space-to-Earth Dual-Use Healthcare: Prolonged spaceflight induces physiological adaptations that mirror accelerated aging, muscle deconditioning, and respiratory or metabolic disorders on Earth. The exact same offline-first clinical assistant and non-invasive breath VOC analyzer can be deployed for firefighters, hazmat responders, divers, remote clinics, and patients managing COPD, asthma, or metabolic conditions.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

·       Frontend & Visualization Stack: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Recharts for real-time physiological sparklines, threshold charts, and a high-contrast medical-aerospace UI, prototyped and hosted through Bolt.

·       AI, Data Modeling & Offline Architecture: Python and PyTorch (LSTM time-series anomaly detection with a +2.0 forget-gate bias for 88% baseline retention across 50 time steps) trained and calibrated using open datasets from NASA OSDR, ALSDA, GeneLab, NLSP, and RadLab; structured around HL7 FHIR healthcare interoperability standards and offline-first local storage/sync architecture (modeled after Apache PouchDB).

·       Hardware & Sensor Interface: Connects via Wi-Fi, Web Bluetooth (BLE), and Serial COM with a handheld multi-sensor Breath VOC Analyzer built around a dual-core ESP32 microcontroller, Sensirion SGP40 metal-oxide VOC gas sensor, Bosch BME280 environmental compensation sensor (temperature, humidity, and pressure), and Sensirion SFM3000 digital mass flow meter.

·       Scientific & Space Agency References: NASA Human Research Program (HRP) Risks & Ongoing Research Roadmap, NASA OSDR / Environmental Data Application (EDA) / RadLab, NASA Life Sciences Portal (NLSP), and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) ISS microgravity and radiation monitoring research.

How the Project Is Creative

·       Time-Series LSTM Breath Curve Analysis: Instead of relying on static single-point averages that miss breath dynamics or mistake sensor drift for medical spikes, our PyTorch LSTM evaluates all 50 sequential readings (sampled every 200 ms over a 10-second breath) with a +2.0 forget-gate bias to lock onto the astronaut's starting baseline from step 1 to step 50.

·       Cascading Continuous-to-Spot-Check Alerting: Separates passive LIVE SENSOR environmental streams (cabin CO2 and radiation) from periodic SPOT-CHECK breath diagnostics, automatically prompting a targeted VOC breath test whenever cabin air quality or radiation levels shift.

·       Real-Time Mission Baseline Injector: Our Sync with OSDR / NLSP data manager lets flight surgeons or judges paste or upload custom NASA JSON/CSV telemetry payloads during a mission or live demo, dynamically recalibrating individualized safety thresholds on the spot without internet access.

·       Built-In Crisis Simulation Lab: Includes four interactive VOC emergency scenarios (Metabolic Crisis: Hepatic Ketosis Surge, Solar Particle Event: Cellular Oxidative Stress, Airway Toxicity: Lunar Dust & Suit Off-Gassing, and Microgravity Deconditioning: Muscle Catabolism) so users and evaluators can test how the system triages multi-system anomalies and guides non-doctors through life-saving protocols.

Factors Considered by Our Team

·       Human Factors & Microgravity Usability: Because astronauts are not physicians and may operate under fatigue or high stress, we engineered a clean, high-contrast medical-aerospace theme with large touch targets, color-coded severity badges, a static anatomical Body Map (avoiding floating animations that can aggravate space motion sickness), and plain-English 3-step instructions.

·       Communication Delays & Offline Resilience: Accounting for signal latencies of up to 22 minutes each way on Mars missions, every AI threshold check, sensor stream, and clinical protocol executes 100% locally offline, queuing logs for asynchronous Earth synchronization whenever bandwidth is available.

·       Operational Realism in Space Medicine: Astronauts cannot run bulky blood chemistry labs in microgravity; pairing lightweight environmental monitoring with a 10-second handheld breathalyzer provides realistic, zero-consumable diagnostics.

·       Evidence-Based Space Physiology: Every biomarker threshold, organ hotspot, and countermeasure (including carbohydrate replenishment for ketosis, HEPA/activated carbon scrubbing for aldehyde airway irritation, storm-shelter protocols for Solar Particle Events, and workload adjustments for muscular strain) was mapped directly to peer-reviewed clinical literature and documented NASA HRP and CSA spaceflight research.
